reflexively.","printedPage":229,"pdfPage":247,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":76},{"text":"One kind of proprioceptor is the muscle spindle, a Do humans have any built-in motor programs?","printedPage":231,"pdfPage":249,"kind":"source_selected_detail","paragraphIndex":120086,"sourceEdition":"Kalat_14e"},{"text":"They’re also presented in alphabetical order with definitions in the book’s Subject Index/Glossary.","printedPage":231,"pdfPage":249,"kind":"source_selected_detail","paragraphIndex":120087,"sourceEdition":"Kalat_14e"},{"text":"Would you expect jaguars, cheetahs, and other great cats to have mostly slow-twitch, nonfatiguing muscles in their legs or mostly fast-twitch, quickly fatiguing muscles?","printedPage":232,"pdfPage":250,"kind":"source_selected_detail","paragraphIndex":120088,"sourceEdition":"Kalat_14e"}],"sourceBodyWords":311,"addedWords":138,"sourceParagraphs":4}],"masterclassCount":1},{"id":"bp14-m7-2","chapterId":"bp14-ch07","moduleId":"bp14-m7-2","moduleNumber":"7.2","title":"Brain Mechanisms of Movement","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":233,"printedEnd":248,"pdfStart":251,"pdfEnd":266,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Movement control relies on the cerebral cortex, pathways to the spinal cord, the cerebellum, and the basal ganglia. These systems contribute to planning, executing, adjusting, and inhibiting movements."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The connections between motor activity and cognition are important here. Compare how the cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia contribute, rather than attributing movement to a single motor center."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-1","text":"Planning and selection"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Premotor and related cortical regions help organize actions before and during execution. Motor cortex influences descending pathways that reach the spinal cord, but movement preparation also includes deciding whether to act. Prefrontal processes help with goals and inhibition: holding back an impulsive movement can be part of successful control. The nervous system considers expected outcomes, current sensory conditions, and learned habits when selecting an action."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-2","text":"Descending signals and spinal circuits"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Commands from the brain reach motor systems through multiple routes, including pathways that influence voluntary limb movement and others important for posture or orienting. The spinal cord is not a passive cable: its circuits organize reflexes and patterns of coordinated muscle activity. Damage at different points in this chain can produce distinct patterns of weakness, loss of control, or altered reflexes."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-3","text":"Cerebellum and basal ganglia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum contributes to timing, coordination, adjustment, and learning of skilled movements. It compares expected and actual consequences and helps refine performance. Basal ganglia circuits have important roles in initiating or selecting actions and regulating their vigor and sequence. The two systems cooperate with cortex but do not perform identical jobs. This distinction becomes especially clear in movement disorders, where the kind of impaired movement depends on the affected network."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-4","text":"Mirror neurons and conscious decisions"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Certain neurons respond both during an action and during observation of similar actions, prompting hypotheses about action understanding. Those hypotheses need careful evaluation: a neural response alone does not prove a sweeping explanation of empathy, imitation, or social behavior. Studies of movement preparation also show that brain activity can precede a person's report of consciously deciding to act. That finding raises questions about timing and awareness without simply settling the philosophical debate about free will."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h01","text":"The Cerebral Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Axons from the motor cortex do not go directly to the muscles, but to the brainstem and spinal cord, which send impulses to the muscles .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although each hemisphere mainly controls the muscles on the contralateral side, both hemispheres contribute to planning movements on both sides .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebral cortex is necessary for complex actions such as talking or writing, but not for coughing, sneezing, gagging, laughing, or crying .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The lack of cerebral control may explain why it is hard to perform those actions voluntarily.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The motor cortex is just anterior to the somatosensory cortex, and the two match up nicely.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Within any area of the motor cortex, the organization represents coordinated movements, not just single muscle contractions.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For many years, researchers studied the motor cortex in laboratory animals by stimulating neurons with brief electrical pulses, usually less than 50 milliseconds (ms) in duration, producing brief muscle twitches.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Later researchers found different results when they lengthened the pulses to half a second.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The motor cortex orders an outcome and leaves it to the spinal cord and other areas to find the right combination of muscles .","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h02","text":"Planning a Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After more intense stimulation at the same locations, people report that they believe they did make the movement—although, in fact, they did not .","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers sometimes use fMRI to measure brain responses while people are preparing to make a movement.","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Or people see a first signal with partial information about what they will have to do, and after a","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In each case, the posterior parietal cortex is active during the delay, evidently preparing the movement .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The supplementary motor cortex in the prefrontal cortex is also essential for planning and organizing movements.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After mild electrical stimulation of the supplementary motor cortex, people report an urge or desire to make a movement, and after stronger stimulation, they actually make a movement .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Activity in the supplementary motor cortex begins at least a second before the start of a voluntary movement and builds up gradually .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It receives information about the target to which the body is directing its movement, as well as information about the body’s current position and posture .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Both kinds of information are necessary to direct a movement toward a target.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parts of the prefrontal cortex are important for considering the probable outcomes of movements .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h03","text":"Inhibiting a Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Or you start to swing at a tennis ball in a doubles match when your partner shouts, “let it go,” because it will land out of bounds.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In cases like these, two brain areas are sending competing messages, and the outcome depends on whether the stop message arrives in time to cancel the action message .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another example—not an important behavior for its own sake, but a convenient one for psychologists to study— is the antisaccade task .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A saccade (sa-KAHD) is a voluntary eye movement from one target to another.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People generally agree that it is easier to look at the finger that moved than the finger that didn’t.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Before age 5 to 7 years, most children find it almost impossible to look away from the wiggling finger.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That is, the brain prepares to inhibit the unwanted action and substitute a different one.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h04","text":"Mirror Neurons"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A discovery in neuroscience that excited many psychologists was mirror neurons , which are active both during a movement and while watching someone else perform the same movement .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mirror neurons were first reported in the premotor cortex of monkeys and later in other areas and other species, including humans .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The theoretical interest comes from the possibility that we use mirror neurons to understand other people or to identify with them.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One speculation was that a lack of mirror neurons might be responsible for autism or schizophrenia, disorders associated with deficient social relationships.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If mirror neurons are going to explain imitation or empathy, the mirror neurons would have to come first.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The only evidence for inborn mirror neurons came from reports that some newborn infants imitate certain adult facial expressions, such as tongue protrusion.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A review of the literature over decades found that six research groups have reported positive findings, whereas 10 groups have not .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mirror neurons are activated not only by seeing an action but also by any reminder of the action, such as hearing an action or reading about it .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h05","text":"From the Brain to the Spinal Cord"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Messages from the brain must reach the medulla and spinal cord, which control the muscles.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Paths from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord are called the corticospinal tracts .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The lateral corticospinal tract extends from the primary motor cortex, nearby areas of the cortex, and the","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The medial corticospinal tract extends from many areas of the cerebral cortex, as well as from several areas of the midbrain and medulla (Figure 7.11).","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Axons of the medial tract go to both sides of the spinal cord about equally, where they control the muscles of the neck, shoulders, and trunk and therefore movements as walking, turning, bending, standing up, and sitting down .","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An easy way to remember the functions of the lateral and medial tracts is that the lateral tract controls muscles in the lateral parts of the body, such as hands and feet.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Note that both paths cross in the medulla and that the touch information arrives at brain areas side by side with those areas responsible for motor control.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, someone with impaired control of the hand muscles might move the shoulders and trunk in a way that repositions the hand.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h06","text":"The Cerebellum"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The term cerebellum is Latin for “little brain.” Decades ago, most texts described the function of the cerebellum as “balance and coordination.” Well, yes, people with cerebellar damage do lose balance and coordination, but that description understates the importance of this structure.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum has more neurons than the rest of the brain combined , a huge number of synapses, and many functions.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum is essential for any behavior that relates to aim or precise timing of short intervals.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Here is a quick way to test the cerebellum: Hold up your hands and ask someone to look at one hand and then quickly look to the other hand.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This move function depends on the cerebellar cortex (the surface of the cerebellum), which sends messages to the cerebellar nuclei (clusters of cell bodies) in the interior of the cerebellum (Figure 7.13).","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This hold function depends on the nuclei alone .","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Finally, the finger moves to the nose by a slower movement that does not depend on the cerebellum.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A police officer testing someone for drunkenness may use the finger-to-nose test or similar tests because the cerebellum is one of the first brain areas that alcohol affects.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h07","text":"Cellular Organization"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum receives input from the spinal cord, from the sensory systems, and from the cerebral cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Processing in the cerebellum finally reaches the cerebellar nuclei, which send output back to the cerebral cortex as well as to downstream targets (Figure 7.14).","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h08","text":"Functions Other than Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditionally, the cerebellum has been emphasized for its role in movement, but it has reciprocal connections with all parts of the cerebral cortex, enabling it to contribute to almost everything the brain does .","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The chapter on learning and memory will discuss the role of the cerebellum in classical conditioning.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In one study, people were told to keep their eyes fixated on a central point.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At various times, they would see the letter E on either the left or right half of the screen, and they were to indicate the direction in which it was oriented (E,","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the circuit diagram of cells in the cerebellum is nearly uniform throughout, researchers and theorists have tried to describe a single function for the cerebellum, but so far without notable success.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Perhaps it is no more reasonable to seek “the” function of the cerebellum than to seek “the” function of the cerebral cortex .","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h09","text":"The Basal Ganglia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The direct pathway from the striatum inhibits the globus pallidus, which inhibits part of the thalamus.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Neuroscientists long believed that the direct pathway stimulates movements whereas the indirect pathway inhibits them.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, later evidence found that both pathways are active before a movement and neither is active when the animal is at rest .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A popular hypothesis is that the direct pathway enhances the selected movement whereas the indirect pathway inhibits competing movements .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This path inhibits actions quickly, when it is important to change plans suddenly .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In trials when it heard a signal indicating exactly when to move, the basal ganglia exhibited little activity.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In another study, people used a computer mouse to draw lines on a screen while researchers used PET scans to examine brain activity.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Activity in the basal ganglia increased when people drew a new line but not when they traced a line already on the screen .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because cells in the primary motor cortex become active before those in the basal ganglia, the basal ganglia must not be responsible for selecting which movement to make.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many cells in the basal ganglia cells respond strongly to signals indicating that a response will probably lead to reward.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Separate sections of the basal ganglia respond to the recent value associated with a stimulus and the long-term average value associated with it .","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cells in the basal ganglia store longterm memories of the reward value of many objects, more than 90 in one study .","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h10","text":"Conscious Decisions and Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each of us has the feeling, “I consciously decide to do something, and then I do it.” It seems so obvious that we might not even question it, but research casts doubt on this assumption.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"On the average, people report that their decision to move occurred about 200 ms before the actual movement. (The decision occurred then.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People report it later.) For example, if you reported that your decision to move occurred at position 25, your decision came 200 ms before the movement that began at position 30. (Remember, the light moves around the circle in 2.56 seconds.) However, your motor cortex produces a kind of activity called a","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"readiness potential for any voluntary movement, and on average, the readiness potential begins at least 500 ms before the movement.","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The research has been replicated in other laboratories, so the results are solid .","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One study found that some neurons in the supplementary motor cortex begin activating more than a second before the reported time of the decision .","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many have assumed that if people can accurately state the time of a stimulus or a movement, they are equally accurate at stating the time of a conscious decision.","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Remember, the letters changed only twice a second, so it wasn’t possible to determine the time of decision with great accuracy.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, it wasn’t necessary, because parts of the frontal and parietal cortices showed activity specific to the left or right hand 7 to 10 seconds before the response .","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h11","text":"In Closing: Movement Control and Cognition"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is tempting to describe behavior in three steps—first we perceive, then we think, and finally we act.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum has traditionally been considered a major part of the motor system, but it is now known to be important in timing sensory processes.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with basal ganglia damage are slow to start a movement, and they are also slow at making any kind of choice.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Organizing a movement is not something we tack on at the end of our thinking.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"develops gradually, because the movement is self-initiated, the type that depends on the basal ganglia .","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Human infants are at first limited to gross movements of the trunk, arms, and legs.","sourcePrintedPage":247,"sourcePdfPage":265,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"Since the pioneering work of Gustav Fritsch and Eduard Hitzig (1870), neuroscientists have known that direct electrical stimulation of the primary motor cortex — the precentral gyrus of the frontal cortex, just anterior to the central sulcus—elicits movements.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Controlling movement also depends on connections between the cortex and subcortical areas, as illustrated in Figure 7.9.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.10 (which repeats parts of Figure 3.23) depicts which areas of the somatosensory cortex feel parts of the body, and which areas of the motor cortex control parts of the body.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, some of the cells in the hand area control grasping movements and others control movements to release a grip.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Stimulation of one spot caused a monkey to make a grasping movement with its hand, move its hand to just in front of the mouth, and open its mouth— as if it were picking up something and preparing to eat it.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"Physicians sometimes perform brain surgery on people who are awake, anesthetizing only the skin of the scalp.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"The details vary, but the general idea is that people detect a first signal that tells them what they are supposed to do, and then they wait for a second signal that indicates make the movement now.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is also essential for inhibiting a habitual movement when you want to do something else, and for learning to correct errors of movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you imagine how a movement would feel, you activate your premotor cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you had damage to this area, many of your movements would be disorganized, such as showering with your clothes on or pouring water on the tube of toothpaste instead of the toothbrush.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you do something absentminded first thing in the morning, probably your prefrontal cortex is not fully awake.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"Consider what happens when you need to restrain an impulse.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"The traffic light changes from red to green, but just as you are about to drive forward, you hear an ambulance siren telling you to stay out of the way.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"Suppose a person is staring straight ahead when something to one side or the other moves.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"Performance declines in old age and as a result of schizophrenia, attention-deficit disorder, or alcohol intoxication.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, certain neurons become active both when people smile and when they see someone else smile.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"That result suggests built-in mirror neurons that connect the sight of a movement to the movement itself.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"After some practice, these “mirror” neurons turned into “counter-mirror” neurons that responded to moving one finger and watching a different finger.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"We have two such tracts, the lateral and medial corticospinal tracts.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"Diseases of the spinal cord impair movement, as listed in Table 7.1.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256},{"type":"bullet","text":"In bulges of the medulla called pyramids, the lateral tract crosses to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256},{"type":"bullet","text":"You may be able to move your fingers on just one side of the body, but movements such as standing, sitting, or turning necessarily include both sides.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.12 compares the lateral tract to the spinal pathway bringing touch information to the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"For a person to control their hands, they have to know where they are and what they are doing now.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"If a stroke damages the primary motor cortex of one hemisphere, the result is impaired movement on the other side of the body.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"It receives input from the cerebral cortex, especially the frontal and parietal lobes, and relays information back to modify cortical activity.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with cerebellar damage can accurately judge the loudness of a sound, but not its duration.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"The eyes make many short movements until, by trial and error, they eventually find the intended spot.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"In the finger-to-nose test, someone is instructed to hold one arm straight out and then, at command, touch the nose as quickly as possible.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.15 is a simplified diagram of neurons in the cerebellum.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sometimes, they saw a signal telling where the letter would be on the screen.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"For most people, that signal improved their performance even if it appeared just 100 ms before the letter.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The cerebellum contributes to many tasks that have little to do with one another.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The term basal ganglia applies to the subcortical forebrain structures illustrated in Figure 7.16.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"( Ganglia is the plural of ganglion.) These structures include the caudate nucleus, the putamen (pyuh-TAY-men), the globus pallidus, and the nucleus accumbens.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The illustration shows the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, a monkey in one study was trained to move a hand left or right to receive food.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"Again, the basal ganglia seem critical for selfinitiated actions, not for stimulus-elicited actions.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"If someone shouts, “Time for dinner,” you get up at once and head for the table.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"Describing the role of the basal ganglia in these terms makes sense of what we see in patients with damage to the basal ganglia, as in Parkinson’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with basal ganglia damage are impaired at learning motor skills and converting them into smooth, automatic responses.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"You don’t choose which movement to make, but you choose the time freely.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"NOW!” You note where the spot was at that critical instant and report, “I made my decision when the light was at position 25.” The researchers compare your report to their records of your brain activity and your wrist movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"In this example, it would start when the light was at position 18, as illustrated in Figure 7.19.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"The results seem to indicate that your conscious decision does not cause your action.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"Rather, you become conscious of the decision after the process leading to action has been underway for about 300 milliseconds.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"Someone monitoring your cortex could, in this situation, predict your choice a few seconds before you were aware of making the decision.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"Nevertheless, your brain activity does not always start 7 to 10 seconds before you make a movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is intimately intertwined with all of our sensory and cognitive processes.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"The study of movement is not just the study of muscles.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you report the time of the decision, it may be little more than a guess.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"Reporting when you decided to make a voluntary movement is like reporting when you fell in love with someone: You know when you were sure of it, or when you first said, “I love you,” but the process was developing gradually long before that.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"The ability to move one finger at a time matures gradually over at least the first year.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":247,"sourcePdfPage":265}],"topicIds":["bp14-m7-2-h01","bp14-m7-2-h02","bp14-m7-2-h03","bp14-m7-2-h04","bp14-m7-2-h05","bp14-m7-2-h06","bp14-m7-2-h07","bp14-m7-2-h08","bp14-m7-2-h09","bp14-m7-2-h10","bp14-m7-2-h11"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m7-2-study-1","title":"Planning Motor cortex influences descending pathways that reach the spinal cord, but movement preparation also includes deciding whether to act. Prefrontal processes help with goals and inhibition: holding back an impulsive movement can be part of successful control. The nervous system considers expected outcomes, current sensory conditions, and learned habits when selecting an action.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":233,"sourcePrintedEnd":248,"sourcePdfStart":251,"sourcePdfEnd":266},{"id":"bp14-m7-2-study-2","title":"Descending signals and spinal circuits","text":"Commands from the brain reach motor systems through multiple routes, including pathways that influence voluntary limb movement and others important for posture or orienting. The spinal cord is not a passive cable: its circuits organize reflexes and patterns of coordinated muscle activity. Damage at different points in this chain can produce distinct patterns of weakness, loss of control, or altered reflexes.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":233,"sourcePrintedEnd":248,"sourcePdfStart":251,"sourcePdfEnd":266},{"id":"bp14-m7-2-study-3","title":"Cerebellum and basal ganglia","text":"The cerebellum contributes to timing, coordination, adjustment, and learning of skilled movements. The two systems cooperate with cortex but do not perform identical jobs. Studies of movement preparation also show that brain activity can precede a person's report of consciously deciding to act. .","printedPage":237,"pdfPage":255,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Mirror neurons are activated not only by seeing an action but also .","printedPage":237,"pdfPage":255,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"For example, certain neurons become active both when people smile the corticospinal tracts .","printedPage":237,"pdfPage":255,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":50},{"text":"The lateral corticospinal tract extends from the primary motor cortex, nearby areas of the cortex, and the","printedPage":238,"pdfPage":256,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51},{"text":"The medial corticospinal tract extends from many areas of the cerebral cortex, as well as from several areas of the midbrain and medulla (Figure 7.11).","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"Axons of the medial tract go to both sides of the spinal cord about equally, where they control the muscles of the neck, shoulders, and trunk and therefore movements as walking, turning, bending, standing up, and sitting down .","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"An easy way to remember the functions of the lateral and medial tracts is that the lateral tract controls muscles in the lateral parts of the body, such as hands and feet.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"Note that both paths cross in the medulla and that the touch information arrives at brain areas side by side with those areas responsible for motor control.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"For example, someone with impaired control of the hand muscles might move the shoulders and trunk in a way that repositions the hand.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"We have two such tracts, the lateral and medial corticospinal tracts.","printedPage":237,"pdfPage":255,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":124},{"text":"Diseases of the spinal cord impair movement, as listed in Table 7.1.","printedPage":238,"pdfPage":256,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":125},{"text":"In bulges of the medulla called pyramids, the lateral tract crosses to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.","printedPage":238,"pdfPage":256,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":126},{"text":"You may be able to move your fingers on just one side of the body, but movements such as standing, sitting, or turning necessarily include both sides.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":127},{"text":"Figure 7.12 compares the lateral tract to the spinal pathway bringing touch information to the cortex.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":128},{"text":"For a person to control their hands, they have to know where they are and what they are doing now.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":129},{"text":"If a stroke damages the primary motor cortex of one hemisphere, the result is impaired movement on the other side of the Cerebellum","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"facts":[{"text":"The term cerebellum is Latin for “little brain.” Decades ago, most texts described the function of the cerebellum as “balance and coordination.” Well, yes, people with cerebellar damage do lose balance and coordination, but that description understates the importance of this structure.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":58},{"text":"The cerebellum has more neurons than the rest of the brain combined , a huge number of synapses, and many functions.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":59},{"text":"The cerebellum is essential for any behavior that relates to aim or precise timing of short intervals.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":60},{"text":"Here is a quick way to test the cerebellum: Hold up your hands and ask someone to look at one hand and then quickly look to the other hand.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":61},{"text":"This move function depends on the cerebellar cortex (the surface of the cerebellum), which sends messages to the cerebellar nuclei (clusters of cell bodies) in the interior of the cerebellum (Figure 7.13).","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"This hold function depends on the nuclei alone .","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":63},{"text":"Finally, the finger moves to the nose by a slower movement that does not depend on the cerebellum.","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"A police officer testing someone for drunkenness may use the finger-to-nose test or similar tests because the cerebellum is one of the first brain areas that alcohol affects.","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"It receives input from the cerebral cortex, especially the frontal and parietal lobes, and relays information back to modify cortical activity.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":131},{"text":"People with cerebellar damage can accurately judge the loudness of a sound, but not its duration.","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":132},{"text":"The eyes make many short movements until, by trial and error, they eventually find the intended spot.","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":133},{"text":"In the finger-to-nose test, someone is instructed to hold one arm straight out and then, at command, touch the nose as quickly as possible.","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":134}],"originalFacts":8,"additionalFacts":4,"glossary":[{"term":"Cerebellum","definition":"highly cortex.","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":67},{"text":"Processing in the cerebellum finally reaches the cerebellar 7.14).","printedPage":240,"pdfPage":258,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":68},{"text":"Figure 7.15 is a simplified diagram of neurons in the Other than Movement","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"facts":[{"text":"Traditionally, the cerebellum has been emphasized for its role in movement, but it has reciprocal connections with all parts of the cerebral cortex, enabling it to contribute to almost everything the brain does .","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":70},{"text":"The chapter on learning and memory will discuss the role of the cerebellum in classical conditioning.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":71},{"text":"In one study, people were told to keep their eyes fixated on a central point.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":72},{"text":"At various times, they would see the letter E on either the left or right half of the screen, and they were to indicate the direction in which it was oriented (E,","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":73},{"text":"Because the circuit diagram of cells in the cerebellum is nearly uniform throughout, researchers and theorists have tried to describe a single function for the cerebellum, but so far without notable success.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":74},{"text":"Perhaps it is no more reasonable to seek “the” function of the cerebellum than to seek “the” function of the cerebral cortex .","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":75},{"text":"Sometimes, they saw a signal telling where the letter would be on the screen.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":136},{"text":"For most people, that signal improved their performance even if it appeared just 100 ms before the letter.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":137},{"text":"The cerebellum contributes to many tasks that have little to do with one another.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":138}],"originalFacts":6,"additionalFacts":3,"glossary":[{"term":"Classical conditioning","definition":"type of conditioning produced by the pairing of two stimuli, one of which evokes an automatic response","sourcePrintedPage":621,"sourcePdfPage":639},{"term":"Cerebral Basal Ganglia","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"facts":[{"text":"The direct pathway from the striatum inhibits the globus pallidus, which inhibits part of the thalamus.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":77},{"text":"Neuroscientists long believed that the direct pathway stimulates movements whereas the indirect pathway inhibits them.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":78},{"text":"However, later evidence found that both pathways are active before a movement and neither is active when the animal is at rest .","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":79},{"text":"A popular hypothesis is that the direct pathway enhances the selected movement whereas the indirect pathway inhibits competing movements .","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":80},{"text":"This path inhibits actions quickly, when it is important to change plans suddenly .","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":81},{"text":"In trials when it heard a signal indicating exactly when to move, the basal ganglia exhibited little activity.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":82},{"text":"In another study, people used a computer mouse to draw lines on a screen while researchers used PET scans to examine brain activity.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":83},{"text":"Activity in the basal ganglia increased when people drew a new line but not when they traced a line already on the screen .","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":84},{"text":"Because cells in the primary motor cortex become active before those in the basal ganglia, the basal ganglia must not be responsible for selecting which movement to make.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":85},{"text":"Many cells in the basal ganglia cells respond strongly to signals indicating that a response will probably lead to reward.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"Separate sections of the basal ganglia respond to the recent value associated with a stimulus and the long-term average value associated with it .","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":87},{"text":"Cells in the basal ganglia store longterm memories of the reward value of many objects, more than 90 in one study .","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":88},{"text":"The term basal ganglia applies to the subcortical forebrain structures illustrated in Figure 7.16.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":139},{"text":"( Ganglia is the plural of ganglion.) These structures include the caudate nucleus, the putamen (pyuh-TAY-men), the globus pallidus, and the nucleus accumbens.","printedPage":242,"pdfPage":260,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":140},{"text":"The illustration shows the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":141},{"text":"For example, a monkey in one study was trained to move a hand left or right to receive food.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":142},{"text":"Again, the basal ganglia seem critical for selfinitiated actions, not for stimulus-elicited actions.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":143},{"text":"If someone shouts, “Time for dinner,” you get up at once and head for the table.","printedPage":243,"pdfPage":261,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":144},{"text":"Describing the role of the basal ganglia in these terms makes sense of what we see in patients with damage to the basal ganglia, as in Parkinson’s disease.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":145},{"text":"People with basal ganglia damage are impaired at learning motor skills and converting them into smooth, automatic responses.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":146}],"originalFacts":12,"additionalFacts":8,"glossary":[{"term":"Basal obvious that we might not even question it, but research casts doubt on this assumption.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":90},{"text":"On the average, people report that their decision to move occurred about 200 ms before the actual movement. (The decision occurred then.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":91},{"text":"People report it later.) For example, if you reported that your decision to move occurred at position 25, your decision came 200 ms before the movement that began at position 30. (Remember, the light moves around the circle in 2.56 seconds.) However, your motor cortex produces a kind of activity called a","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":92},{"text":"readiness potential for any voluntary movement, and on average, the readiness potential begins at least 500 ms before the movement.","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":93},{"text":"The research has been replicated in other laboratories, so the results are solid .","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":94},{"text":"One study found that some neurons in the supplementary motor cortex begin activating more than a second before the reported time of the decision .","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":95},{"text":"Many have assumed that if people can accurately state the time of a stimulus or a movement, they are equally accurate at stating the time of a conscious decision.","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":96},{"text":"Remember, the letters changed only twice a second, so it wasn’t possible to determine the time of decision with great accuracy.","printedPage":246,"pdfPage":264,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":97},{"text":"However, it wasn’t necessary, because parts of the frontal and parietal cortices showed activity specific to the left or right hand 7 to 10 seconds before the response .","printedPage":246,"pdfPage":264,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":98},{"text":"You don’t choose which movement to make, but you choose the time freely.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":147},{"text":"NOW!” You note where the spot was at that critical instant and report, “I made my decision when the light was at position 25.” The researchers compare your report to their records of your brain activity and your wrist movement.","printedPage":244,"pdfPage":262,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":148},{"text":"In this example, it would start when the light was at position 18, as illustrated in Figure 7.19.","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":149},{"text":"The results seem to indicate that your conscious decision does not cause your action.","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":150},{"text":"Rather, you become conscious of the decision after the process leading to action has been underway for about 300 milliseconds.","printedPage":245,"pdfPage":263,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":151},{"text":"Someone monitoring your cortex could, in this situation, predict your choice a few seconds before you were aware of making the decision.","printedPage":246,"pdfPage":264,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":152},{"text":"Nevertheless, your brain activity does not always start 7 to 10 seconds before you make a may be little more than a guess.","printedPage":246,"pdfPage":264,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":156},{"text":"Reporting when you decided to Later researchers found different results when they lengthened the pulses to half a second.","The motor cortex orders an outcome and leaves it to the spinal cord and other areas to find the right combination of muscles.","After more intense stimulation at the same locations, people report that they believe they did make the movement—although, in fact, they did not.","Researchers sometimes use fMRI to measure brain responses while people are preparing to make a movement.","Or people see a first signal with partial information about what they will have to do, and after a","In each case, the posterior parietal cortex is active during the delay, evidently preparing the movement. The supplementary motor cortex in the prefrontal cortex is also essential for planning and organizing movements.","After mild electrical stimulation of the supplementary motor cortex, people report an urge or desire to make a movement, and after stronger stimulation, they actually make a movement.","Activity in the supplementary motor cortex begins at least a second before the start of a voluntary movement and builds up gradually.","It receives information about the target to which the body is directing its movement, as well as information about the body’s current position and posture. Both kinds of information are necessary to direct a movement toward a target.","Parts of the prefrontal cortex are important for considering the probable outcomes of movements.","Or you start to swing at a tennis ball in a doubles match when your partner shouts, “let it go,” because it will land out of bounds.","In cases like these, two brain areas are sending competing messages, and the outcome depends on whether the stop message arrives in time to cancel the action message.","Another example—not an important behavior for its own sake, but a convenient one for psychologists to study— is the antisaccade task. A saccade (sa-KAHD) is a voluntary eye movement from one target to another.","People generally agree that it is easier to look at the finger that moved than the finger that didn’t.","Before age 5 to 7 years, most children find it almost impossible to look away from the wiggling finger. That is, the brain prepares to inhibit the unwanted action and substitute a different one.","A discovery in neuroscience that excited many psychologists was mirror neurons, which are active both during a movement and while watching someone else perform the same movement.","Mirror neurons were first reported in the premotor cortex of monkeys and later in other areas and other species, including humans.","The theoretical interest comes from the possibility that we use mirror neurons to understand other people or to identify with them. One speculation was that a lack of mirror neurons might be responsible for autism or schizophrenia, disorders associated with deficient social relationships.","If mirror neurons are going to explain imitation or empathy, the mirror neurons would have to come first.","The only evidence for inborn mirror neurons came from reports that some newborn infants imitate certain adult facial expressions, such as tongue protrusion.","A review of the literature over decades found that six research groups have reported positive findings, whereas 10 groups have not. Mirror neurons are activated not only by seeing an action but also by any reminder of the action, such as hearing an action or reading about it.","Messages from the brain must reach the medulla and spinal cord, which control the muscles.","Paths from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord are called the corticospinal tracts.","The lateral corticospinal tract extends from the primary motor cortex, nearby areas of the cortex, and the The medial corticospinal tract extends from many areas of the cerebral cortex, as well as from several areas of the midbrain and medulla (Figure 7.11).","Axons of the medial tract go to both sides of the spinal cord about equally, where they control the muscles of the neck, shoulders, and trunk and therefore movements as walking, turning, bending, standing up, and sitting down.","An easy way to remember the functions of the lateral and medial tracts is that the lateral tract controls muscles in the lateral parts of the body, such as hands and feet.","Note that both paths cross in the medulla and that the touch information arrives at brain areas side by side with those areas responsible for motor control. For example, someone with impaired control of the hand muscles might move the shoulders and trunk in a way that repositions the hand.","The term cerebellum is Latin for “little brain.” Decades ago, most texts described the function of the cerebellum as “balance and coordination.” Well, yes, people with cerebellar damage do lose balance and coordination, but that description understates the importance of this structure.","The cerebellum has more neurons than the rest of the brain combined, a huge number of synapses, and many functions.","The cerebellum is essential for any behavior that relates to aim or precise timing of short intervals. Here is a quick way to test the cerebellum: Hold up your hands and ask someone to look at one hand and then quickly look to the other hand.","This move function depends on the cerebellar cortex (the surface of the cerebellum), which sends messages to the cerebellar nuclei (clusters of cell bodies) in the interior of the cerebellum (Figure 7.13).","This hold function depends on the nuclei alone.","Finally, the finger moves to the nose by a slower movement that does not depend on the cerebellum. A police officer testing someone for drunkenness may use the finger-to-nose test or similar tests because the cerebellum is one of the first brain areas that alcohol affects.","The cerebellum processes information through a highly organized circuit. It receives signals from the spinal cord, sensory systems, and cerebral cortex; these pathways converge on cerebellar circuits, whose output helps regulate activity elsewhere in the brain.","Motor-related signals from the cerebral cortex reach the cerebellum through the pons. Sensory and spinal inputs also supply information about the ongoing state of the body.","Traditionally, the cerebellum has been emphasized for its role in movement, but it has reciprocal connections with all parts of the cerebral cortex, enabling it to contribute to almost everything the brain does.","The chapter on learning and memory will discuss the role of the cerebellum in classical conditioning.","In one study, people were told to keep their eyes fixated on a central point.","At various times, they would see the letter E on either the left or right half of the screen, and they were to indicate the direction in which it was oriented (E, Because the circuit diagram of cells in the cerebellum is nearly uniform throughout, researchers and theorists have tried to describe a single function for the cerebellum, but so far without notable success.","Perhaps it is no more reasonable to seek “the” function of the cerebellum than to seek “the” function of the cerebral cortex.","The direct pathway from the striatum inhibits the globus pallidus, which inhibits part of the thalamus.","Neuroscientists long believed that the direct pathway stimulates movements whereas the indirect pathway inhibits them.","However, later evidence found that both pathways are active before a movement and neither is active when the animal is at rest. A popular hypothesis is that the direct pathway enhances the selected movement whereas the indirect pathway inhibits competing movements.","This path inhibits actions quickly, when it is important to change plans suddenly.","In trials when it heard a signal indicating exactly when to move, the basal ganglia exhibited little activity. In another study, people used a computer mouse to draw lines on a screen while researchers used PET scans to examine brain activity.","Activity in the basal ganglia increased when people drew a new line but not when they traced a line already on the screen. Because cells in the primary motor cortex become active before those in the basal ganglia, the basal ganglia must not be responsible for selecting which movement to make.","Many cells in the basal ganglia cells respond strongly to signals indicating that a response will probably lead to reward.","Separate sections of the basal ganglia respond to the recent value associated with a stimulus and the long-term average value associated with it. Cells in the basal ganglia store longterm memories of the reward value of many objects, more than 90 in one study.","Each of us has the feeling, “I consciously decide to do something, and then I do it.” It seems so obvious that we might not even question it, but research casts doubt on this assumption.","On the average, people report that their decision to move occurred about 200 ms before the actual movement. (The decision occurred then.","People report it later.) For example, if you reported that your decision to move occurred at position 25, your decision came 200 ms before the movement that began at position 30. (Remember, the light moves around the circle in 2.56 seconds.) However, your motor cortex produces a kind of activity called a","readiness potential for any voluntary movement, and on average, the readiness potential begins at least 500 ms before the movement. The research has been replicated in other laboratories, so the results are solid.","One study found that some neurons in the supplementary motor cortex begin activating more than a second before the reported time of the decision.","Many have assumed that if people can accurately state the time of a stimulus or a movement, they are equally accurate at stating the time of a conscious decision. Remember, the letters changed only twice a second, so it wasn’t possible to determine the time of decision with great accuracy.","However, it wasn’t necessary, because parts of the frontal and parietal cortices showed activity specific to the left or right hand 7 to 10 seconds before the response.","It is tempting to describe behavior in three steps—first we perceive, then we think, and finally we act.","The cerebellum has traditionally been considered a major part of the motor system, but it is now known to be important in timing sensory processes.","People with basal ganglia damage are slow to start a movement, and they are also slow at making any kind of choice.","Organizing a movement is not something we tack on at the end of our thinking. develops gradually, because the movement is self-initiated, the type that depends on the basal ganglia.","Human infants are at first limited to gross movements of the trunk, arms, and legs.","The important distinction is between input processing in the cerebellar cortex and output from the deep cerebellar nuclei. This arrangement supports the coordination and adjustment of movement.","The cerebellar cortex contains organized circuits including granule cells and Purkinje cells. They transform incoming activity before it influences the output nuclei.","Processing reaches the deep cerebellar nuclei, which send output toward the cerebral cortex through the thalamus and toward other downstream motor centers.","The separation of input, processing, and output provides a framework for understanding how the cerebellum contributes to movement timing, correction, and coordination."],"classroomResearch":{"title":"Evidence in context: The Cerebral Cortex","body":"Later researchers found different results when they lengthened the pulses to half a second.","printedPages":[234],"pdfPages":[252],"kind":"textbook_selected_research","evidenceMethod":"single_verified_textbook_passage"},"classroomCoverage":{"status":"source_structured_full_book","level":"comprehensive_book_derived","topicHeadings":11,"bullets":47,"newWords":1982,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"verified_pdf_topic_facts_crosschecked_with_uploaded_markdown"},"classroomFigures":[{"id":"figure-7-12","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","number":"7.12","title":"Descending motor pathways","printedPage":239,"pdfPage":257,"alt":"Excerpt from Figure 7.12 of Kalat Biological Psychology, showing descending motor pathways.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":496,"height":532,"source":"Cropped figure from user-supplied textbook PDF","cropPdfPoints":[68,473,316,739],"status":"figure number and printed page checked in PDF;
